finding.claim: dropTable discards the result of Authorize(u, "dba"), so any caller that reaches the handler with a context user can run DROP TABLE. Once auth middleware exists, non-DBA users can drop tables.
finding.source: Any request to /admin/drop with a context user; the user is read from context key "user" at api.go:22, and no middleware in this repo sets it.
finding.sink: runSQL("DROP TABLE " + ...) at api.go:27, a destructive schema operation.

trace.note: /admin/drop is registered to dropTable with no middleware.
userFrom does a single-value type assertion on the context value. It panics if the value is nil, which is the case as shipped, so the handler is currently unreachable (net/http recovers the panic).
Authorize(u, "dba") is called and its error is discarded. Execution continues regardless of the role check.

finding.guards_checked: The only role check on the path is api.go:26, and its result is ignored. Authorize (api.go:13-20) fails closed, but its result is not used. vacuum (api.go:33-36) shows the intended pattern. No other middleware or auth exists in the repo. The panic at api.go:22 means the route is not reachable in the current build, so this is latent until auth middleware is added.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize (api.go:13-20) returns an error, not a throw, but its result is discarded at api.go:26, so it is not an effective guard. vacuum (api.go:33-35) checks the result correctly, which shows the intended pattern. The only control that actually blocks the path is the unchecked type assertion at api.go:22: `r.Context().Value("user").(*User)` panics on the nil value, and no code in the repo sets context key "user", so the handler never reaches line 26-27.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code (api.go:26 discards Authorize's error, api.go:27 builds the DROP from r.FormValue("t"), api.go:44 registers the route with no middleware), but api.go:22 panics for every request because nothing sets the "user" context value, so an attacker cannot reach the DROP at api.go:27 in this build; the discarded role check is a real latent authorization defect that only becomes exploitable once middleware sets a user, so it should be reported as latent, not as a current vulnerability.

finding.claim: The table name from the request is concatenated into a DROP TABLE statement with no validation, allowlist, or identifier quoting, which allows SQL injection.
finding.source: r.FormValue("t") at api.go:27, a client-controlled query or form parameter.
finding.sink: runSQL at api.go:27, which executes the concatenated SQL string (stub at api.go:41; actual behavior not visible in repo).

trace.note: r.FormValue("t") is read and concatenated into "DROP TABLE " with no checks.
runSQL is an empty stub, so whether multiple statements execute depends on the driver, which is not in the repo.

finding.guards_checked: None on this path. No allowlist, quoting, or escaping. The authorization issue in F1 does not gate this concatenation, since the result is discarded. Exploitability beyond a single identifier depends on the database driver, which I could not verify.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 is a bare statement, so its error return is discarded and it does not gate the DROP. No allowlist, identifier quoting, parameterization, or escaping exists on the path from r.FormValue("t") at api.go:27 to runSQL at api.go:27. runSQL at api.go:41 is an empty stub, so the sink's real behavior is not in the repo. The authentication middleware that sets the "user" context value is also not in the repo.
verdict.reason: api.go:27 concatenates the client-controlled r.FormValue("t") straight into a "DROP TABLE " SQL string with no validation (api.go:27), and the only role check on the path, Authorize at api.go:26, has its error discarded, so it does not block the request. The caveat is that runSQL (api.go:41) is a stub, so multi-statement or extra-clause exploitation depends on the real driver; the identifier-injection flaw itself is present in the code as written.

finding.claim: runSQL returns nothing, so SQL errors are lost. The handlers still return 204 whether or not the DROP or VACUUM succeeded.
finding.source: Database result from runSQL, called at api.go:27 and api.go:37.
finding.sink: HTTP 204 response at api.go:28 and api.go:38, which tells the caller the operation succeeded.

trace.note: runSQL has no return value, so it cannot report failure.
The VACUUM result is ignored in the same way.

finding.guards_checked: None. The signature of runSQL itself leaves no error path.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. Authorize at api.go:26 is called as a bare statement and its error is discarded, so it blocks nothing. runSQL at api.go:41 is `func runSQL(string) {}` with no return value. dropTable (api.go:28) and vacuum (api.go:38) both return 204 unconditionally after the runSQL call.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: runSQL at api.go:41 has no return value, so the DROP at api.go:27 and VACUUM at api.go:37 results are unobservable, and both handlers write 204 at api.go:28 and api.go:38 regardless of outcome. The claim holds as written, but its severity is low because runSQL is a no-op stub here, and the more serious issue in the same handler is that dropTable discards the Authorize error at api.go:26, so any authenticated user can reach DROP TABLE, which vacuum at api.go:33-35 does not allow.

finding.claim: The admin endpoints are served as plaintext HTTP on all interfaces with default timeouts, and the ListenAndServe error is ignored.
finding.source: Network clients reaching port 8083 on any interface.
finding.sink: Administrative endpoints /admin/drop and /admin/vacuum, whose only protection is the middleware that is absent from this repo.

trace.note: http.ListenAndServe(":8083", nil) binds to all interfaces with no TLS, no read or write timeouts, and an unchecked error return.
/admin/drop is registered and reachable on that listener.
/admin/vacuum is registered and reachable on that listener.

finding.guards_checked: No TLS, no bind-address restriction, no middleware registration, and no timeouts are present in the repo. The unchecked error at line 46 means a bind failure is silent.

verdict.guard_found: In-repo: none for the transport claim (no TLS, bind restriction, or timeouts). api.go:33-36 is an effective check in vacuum() because its error is tested. api.go:26 in dropTable() is a discarded call, so it is not a guard. api.go:22 assumes a "user" context value set by middleware; that middleware is not in the repo.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: api.go:44-46 registers both admin routes on a plaintext ListenAndServe(":8083", nil) with no timeouts and an ignored error. Whether an anonymous client can reach /admin/drop depends on middleware that sets the "user" context value (api.go:22), and that middleware is not in this repo, so the attack path cannot be decided here. Separately, api.go:26 discards the Authorize result, so dropTable has no effective authorization check in this code.
